title: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts
description: Sam's Club and Walmart stores.Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the r
body: Sam's Club and Walmart stores.Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam's Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options."We're giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. "For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own."The membership gives customers access to Sam's Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam's Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.While Walmart's customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam's Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices. In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street. Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it's well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.Meanwhile, Sam's Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period. The membership business — which is part of Walmart's push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam's Club, that revenue number grew 6%.Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits. The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company's fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

schema.headline: Walmart launches joint membership with Sam's Club as it leans into delivery, gas discounts

title: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks
description: A Royal Air Force Typhoon jet taxis out towards the runway at the U.K.'s Liverpool John Lennon airport at sunset ready for takeoff.Wellsie82 | Moment
body: A Royal Air Force Typhoon jet taxis out towards the runway at the U.K.'s Liverpool John Lennon airport at sunset ready for takeoff.Wellsie82 | Moment | Getty ImagesThe U.K. said it would provide defensive military support, including fighter jets, to support Saudi Arabia as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalate.The Houthis, a Yemeni militant group, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets in recent weeks. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage, while facilities belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco were targeted last week. "The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region," U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a statement on Tuesday.New deployment adds to Britain's existing Saudi missionHe added that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles."This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks," Streeting said.The U.K. Ministry of Defence also said that the fighter jets would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis. It said the Royal Air Force would also provide an Airbus A400M Atlas jet "to support the movement of defence materiel within Saudi Arabia," while U.K. military advisers will also give support to Saudi staff officers."Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK — driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen," the MoD said. "We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on civilian targets like King Khalid International Airport and are clear that Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves."Fighting in Yemen intensifies as Iran war reverberatesYemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war.Al Jazeera reported Monday that at least 53 people were killed when the Houthis launched three ballistic missiles at a military camp in southern Yemen. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports.

schema.headline: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi cities from Houthi attacks

title: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis
description: People walk past a sign for Novo Nordisk’s annual general meeting at the entrance to the venue in Copenhagen, Denmark, March 26, 2026.Tom Little | Reu
body: People walk past a sign for Novo Nordisk’s annual general meeting at the entrance to the venue in Copenhagen, Denmark, March 26, 2026.Tom Little | ReutersNovo on Tuesday said its next-generation obesity drug, CagriSema, showed 25% weight loss on average among adult women in a new analysis conducted after a late-stage trial. The Danish company said further work is needed to confirm the hypotheses of two post-study analyses. Still, the results are the latest evidence that the experimental injection can improve upon the weight loss and other benefits offered by Novo's GLP-1 drug semaglutide, the active ingredient in its blockbuster obesity shot Wegovy and diabetes counterpart Ozempic. CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and another drug called cagrilintide that targets the amylin pathway, is expected to launch early next year. Obesity drug leaders Novo and Eli Lilly have built new treatments around amylin, which involves a hormone released in the pancreas alongside insulin that helps regulate hunger and fullness, hoping it will give them a new revenue stream beyond existing GLP-1s. In an analysis of roughly 2,300 women with obesity or who are overweight, CagriSema caused 25% weight loss on average at 68 weeks compared with 3% with placebo. The results are based on an ideal scenario in which all patients stayed on treatment without interruptions. A second analysis of around 1,900 women assigned by their menopausal status found that weight loss reached 26.7%, 24.8%, and 23.1% in premenopausal, perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, respectively, at 68 weeks, if all patients remained on the drug. That compares with approximately 2% across menopause groups with a placebo. Across both analyses, CagriSema was linked to reductions in abdominal fat, based on waist circumference, among women overall and across menopause stages, Novo added. The results suggest that women may experience slightly more weight loss on CagriSema than a broader population of both men and women with obesity saw in the phase 3 trial. Initial results from the study showed that CagriSema helped adults lose 22.7% of their weight on average at 68 weeks versus 2.3% in the placebo group. However, the majority of patients in the trial — around 67% of roughly 3,400 — were women. Weight gain is very common for women during menopause. Declining estrogen levels can contribute to a slowdown in metabolism, making it easier for women to gain weight and harder to maintain muscle mass. After menopause, estrogen generally remains low and does not return to previous levels.More than 86 million women in the U.S. are 40 and older, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, which are the years in which perimenopause, menopause and postmenopause occur. "Many women with obesity or overweight experience weight gain as they move through menopause, and it is important to explore investigational products such as CagriSema across the reproductive lifespan," said Michelle Skinner Moore, Novo's interim head of clinical development, medical and regulatory affairs. Wall Street has not appeared particularly excited about CagriSema, whose previous late-stage clinical trial results disappointed investors because the drug showed weight loss efficacy below their expectations. Novo, however, maintains CagriSema is effective and differentiated enough from its other drugs to draw significant demand.Analysts expect CagriSema to generate $11.84 billion in sales for obesity specifically in 2028, according to a consensus estimate compiled by FactSet.

schema.headline: Novo's next-generation obesity drug shows 25% weight loss in women in late-stage analysis

title: Salesforce announces $5.66 billion deal for Braze, sending BRZE stock soaring 50%
description: Sheldon Cooper | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Salesforce slipped roughly 1% on Tuesday morning, after the company announced an agreement to buy
body: Sheldon Cooper | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Salesforce slipped roughly 1% on Tuesday morning, after the company announced an agreement to buy customer engagement platform Braze for about $5.66 billion.Under the deal, holders of Braze Class A common stock will get $47.50 in cash per share. The transaction is expected to close in fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, according to a Salesforce blog.Braze shares closed at $30.04 on Monday. The stock skyrocketed more than 50% on Tuesday after a brief halt premarket following the news. The company makes artificial intelligence marketing tools to manage customer data and messaging."Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we'll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us," Bill Magnuson, CEO of Braze, said in a statement. "Salesforce's platform will help us innovate faster and together we'll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers."The latest deal comes just months after Salesforce announced it would buy AI customer service platform Fin for about $3.6 billion, in a move meant to bolster the company's agentic AI offerings for enterprises. In August, Salesforce and Anthropic announced an expanded partnership, including a new plugin called "Claudeforce" with pre-built sales skills for salespeople to better compose emails, update records and more with the frontier lab's model. title: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance
description: watch nowDETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-qua
body: watch nowDETROIT — General Motors narrowed its 2026 earnings guidance and raised its free cash flow expectations after beating Wall Street's third-quarter expectations. The Detroit automaker also announced a new multiyear stock buyback of $20 billion after GM completed a $6 billion share repurchase program that was announced in January. GM did not disclose a specific time to complete the program.Despite the positive news, GM stock was off roughly 5% during trading Tuesday as the company's outlook missed Wall Street's expectations.Wall Street analysts were mixed before the report on whether GM would raise its guidance Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs. Analysts' expectations included a midpoint of $13.41 per share for the year compared with GM's new $13.25 per share midpoint, according to LSEG. Several analysts in investor notes Tuesday said GM's third-quarter results were solid, but raised concerns about whether higher costs and pressures on vehicle pricing would limit earnings growth next year.Here's how GM performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.70 adjusted vs. $3.63 expectedRevenue: $50.02 billion vs. $48.7 billion expectedGM's new guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, or $12.75 to $13.75 adjusted earnings per share, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of between $11.5 billion and $12.5 billion.That compares with its raised guidance from July that included adjusted EBIT of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 to $14 adjusted EPS, and adjusted automotive free cash flow of $9.5 billion to $11.5 billion."I think the market's been pretty consistent from what we've said all year," GM CFO Paul Jacobson told CNBC's Phil LeBeau. "Our fourth quarter's going to be down sequentially. ... I think the fact that we're able to hold our guidance in the face of that late inflationary pressure in the year is another sign of the GM team executing really well."Mary Barra, chair and chief executive officer of General Motors Co., during a news conference at the Hudson's building in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Monday, April 15, 2024.Jeff Kowalsky | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesGM on Tuesday said it expects commodity inflation costs to be around $2 billion, which was the high end of its previous guidance. That includes higher costs for logistics and dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, chips that are impacting multiple industries.While the inflationary costs were at the automaker's high end of guidance, GM said its gross tariff costs are expected to be at the low end of its expected $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion range. Warranty costs are expected to be at high end between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, GM said.Jacobson said vehicle pricing is relatively flat as inflationary costs continue to increase. He said the company would assess where consumers are in the coming year when deciding if it should pass costs along by raising prices more than normal."GM is performing well, and we are working hard to continue our momentum despite growing inflationary pressures through strategic investments in new products and services, and through improved quality and operating efficiency," GM CEO Mary Barra said Tuesday in a letter to shareholders.The automaker also said the costs of its pullback in all-electric vehicles announced last year were "substantially completed," saying it has recorded $11.2 billion in such charges since the second half of last year, including paying $4.6 billion of $7.4 billion in cash through the third quarter.The company's net income attributed to stockholders was $3.3 billion during the third quarter, up roughly $2 billion from a year earlier.GM's North American operations continued to lead the automaker's results, accounting for $3.6 billion of its $4.1 billion in adjusted EBIT results during the third quarter.GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.

schema.headline: General Motors beats Wall Street's Q3 earnings expectations, narrows full-year guidance

title: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
description: watch nowOpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI. Bob McGrew's n
body: watch nowOpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI. Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures. Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was also Palantir's product and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril. "It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone."When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster."McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever."OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEO Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, who left to start Anthropic, and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you." McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence. "I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman delivers the keynote address during the OpenAI developers conference at Fort Mason on Sept. 29, 2026 in San Francisco, California. Heather Diehl | Getty ImagesMcGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta, and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick.Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back. "Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high."McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S. "If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said. McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing."No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs."

schema.headline: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing

title: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop
description: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Ima
body: Apple CEO John Ternus during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, Sept. 9, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesApple announced a product launch event on Oct. 28, sending invitations on Monday to media and analysts for an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles." The email says "Pro and tell," suggesting the launch will focus on high-end "Pro" devices with powerful homegrown chips. Ben Reitzes, an analyst at Melius Research, wrote in a note on Monday that he expects new Macs to be introduced, "including a touchscreen notebook," this fall. He said that for CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month, the launch cadence marks a "meaningful shift" from what has been two events a year.Apple's invite to media for the event. AppleIt will be Apple's third launch in Ternus' brief tenure, following an event at company headquarters for new iPhones, including the foldable Duo, and a gathering in New York centered around smart home hubs and a new speaker with a screen called HomeView.Apple updated its Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktops with new chips in August, and refreshed its MacBook Pro in the spring, along with a new low-cost MacBook Neo. But Apple's iMac desktop hasn't been updated since October 2024. In the most recent quarter, Apple's Mac sales accounted for about 10% of overall revenue, as the company remains heavily reliant on iPhones. Still, Macs have become one of the strongest parts of Apple's artificial intelligence story, thanks to its chips that can access more memory at higher speeds than other consumer processors. Apple shares are up 26% so far this year, outperforming the S&P 500. Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops, with software chief Craig Federighi explaining in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. WATCH: Apple and Meta find new common ground in AIwatch now

schema.headline: Apple announces product launch event for Oct. 28. Analysts expect touchscreen laptop

title: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend
description: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, Fra
body: Protestors on the statue of Marianne on the Monument à la République (Statue de la République) during demonstrations on October 17, 2026 in Paris, France. Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesFrance will deploy some military forces to help maintain order during a fresh wave of protests expected this weekend, officials said Tuesday. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers in the National Assembly that the government would ⁠deploy forces from France's Sentinelle force — a domestic military operation that was launched in 2015 following terrorist attacks in Paris — "mainly on static security missions."This would free up police and gendarmes — a military police force — to carry out law enforcement objectives, Nuñez added.Also addressing parliament on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said authorities planned to mobilize a "massive" security presence this coming Saturday, adding that the government's objective was to achieve "an immediate return to order."Lecornu also said there would be fresh curfews "where the situation requires it," according to French newspaper Le Monde. Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, he said earlier on Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes. Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors.The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades.The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027.In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required. Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years.Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country's education system, the cost of living and other issues.While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire.Protesters vandalise a retail store during a demonstration near Paris's Place de la République, as the Gilets Jaunes join students for a weekend of action on Oct. 17, 2026 in Paris, France.Carl Court | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesPolitical commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis." Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation.Businesses hitThere is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday after claiming responsibility for what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed. "The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday."This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said.French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added.Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments. "The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email."Further violence is not inevitable, but protests linked to the underlying grievances, including cost-of-living pressures and discontent over public services and education, are likely to persist, putting continued pressure on the government to demonstrate that it can maintain order," Middleton said.French markets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level. Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

schema.headline: France to deploy military as it braces for fresh unrest this weekend

title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeThe Saudi national accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters was ordered detained without bail pending trial Monday by a San Francisco federal judge who said that there is a "significant" risk he would flee.The order came at a court hearing where Judge Alex Tse sharply questioned the value of an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay the full bail for Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who was working for OpenAI as an engineer when he allegedly planted the device in a television on Sept. 28.Tse said he found the Saudi offer "problematic.""It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out," Tse said in the courtroom, as Alfozan and several dozen of his supporters looked on."The Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.'" Tse noted. "But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?""That he's not going to flee? He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia," the judge said. "He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor."Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States, which the judge referred to at the hearing. Tse also noted that OpenAI has terminated Alfozan.Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted.Tse ordered Alfozan to return to court on Nov. 6.Prosecutors from the San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office during Monday's hearing, and in a detention memo, detailed Alfozan's ties to Saudi Arabia as they argued he was a flight risk. Those ties include his wife and their 3-month-old son, who left the United States shortly after his arrest.Prosecutors in that court filing Sunday said that Alfozan's alleged bugging of the artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."The filing says, "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in the company's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Alfozan planted the device."This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says.Source: U.S. District Court in San Francisco, U.S. v. Alfozan.Prosecutors said in the filing that Alfozan has access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said. "He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.Prosecutors in their filing said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026.Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said.Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person. "Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says."In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote. "The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant.Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined Raed as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.The recording device planted at OpenAI's office, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeProsecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their baby son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12. The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said. Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, told Judge Tse that the defendant was willing to put up $1 million in assets to secure his release, in addition to the Saudi Consulate's offer. A letter from the consulate was included in a motion for pretrial release by Pernik.Pernik had asked Tse to release Alfozan on bail with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13.Pernik, in arguing for Alfozan's release, said the defendant has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit-participating units, his lawyer said in a court filing.Prosecutors in their detention memo said Alfozan had planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12."On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing by prosecutors said.The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.The filing also says that after Alfozan's arrest, his iPhone was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred.""The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in thecustomized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said.OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. The camera was installed after OpenAI discovered the recording device on Sept. 30, prosecutors said.His cellphone also contained a deleted note from September "with links to various recording devices, including devices made by Seeed Studio, the manufacturer of the devices OpenAI found in its offices and the devices FBI agents found in the defendant's residence," the filing said.Another note, entitled "OpenAI leave," suggests that Alfozan planned early pickup "of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full,'" the filing said.In addition to being in contact with a Saudi royal, Alfozan "was pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including participating in the Misk Foundation's '2030 Leaders' program, which would have required his in- person participation in Riyadh," prosecutors said.A day before she left the U.S. with their baby, Alfozan's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia — and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same," the filing said.Alfozan's lawyer, Pernik, in his request that Alfozan be released into home detention, said, "nationality is not evidence of flight," and that his planned travel to Saudi Arabia was for "family and immigration reasons." Alfozan's wife's 60-day post-employment grace period for her own visa was expiring on Oct. 12, the originally scheduled date of their flight, the lawyer said."Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI'spublic statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time."The lawyer also said that Alfozan, who had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia for himself and his family, regularly bought one-way tickets because he has learned they are more cost-effective than changing his flights at the last minute.Pernik also wrote that the Saudi Consulate General confirmed in writing to the U.S. Pretrial Services Office on Thursday that it "'will not issue any travel documents' to Mr. Alfozan during his release and that, if he requests one, it 'undertakes to promptly notify U.S. Pretrial Services.'"The attorney argued that prosecutors have not shown that Alfozan is a serious flight risk."Mr. Alfozan has lived in the United States for fifteen years and in the Bay Area for roughly ten," Pernik wrote. "Fifty-four people, at least twenty-seven of them in the Bay Area, have written to the Court, and they describe someone who organizes dinners, welcomes newcomers, mentors students, and shows up for friends' weddings, birthdays, and moves.""That is not the profile of a person with one foot out the door," Pernik said.— Jordan Novet reported from San Francisco.Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Abdulrahman Alfozan's lawyer is William Pernik. A previous version misspelled Pernik's name.

schema.headline: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan held without bail after Saudi government offers to pay

title: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests
description: Protesters march through central Paris amid fires, smoke, police deployments and clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the high cost of liv
body: Protesters march through central Paris amid fires, smoke, police deployments and clashes during nationwide demonstrations against the high cost of living, on Oct. 17, 2026 in Paris, France.Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesAnger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities.France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers.Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent.There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added. Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check.What sparked the protests?The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services.In Spain, housing protests began in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later. Thousands of protesters also took to the streets in Portugal on Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living. "People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday.watch nowIn Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins. In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades. "The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said. Why now?The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris."This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate."Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with President Emmanuel Macron.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowing France's deficit, projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave."Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added.The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according to Insee, the national statistics bureau. The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%.Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited by Le Monde.Calculations by the French Institute of Economics for Le Monde estimate that the decline in purchasing power since 2024 is equivalent to a loss of 1,200 euros ($1,345) a year for a household with two adults and two children, and 600 euros for a single adult.During the demonstration on 17 October in Limoges protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges Haute-Vienne in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region of France on 17 October 2026. Elise Cabane | Afp | Getty ImagesPortugal's Sarmento said that the situation across Europe varies, with Portugal in a stronger fiscal position and with much less debt than France. "Those countries [those with higher public debt] have much less fiscal margin to act, but the main issue is that we need to resolve the problem of productivity and competitiveness at the European level," he said.      "The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S., and without economic growth, it's impossible to have better salaries and to have the resources for better public services and social support," Sarmento added.In the second quarter of 2026, Portugal recorded the EU's highest annual increase in house prices, up 16.5% from a year earlier, according to Eurostat. The Portuguese government is looking to increase the supply of housing to reduce buying and renting costs to resolve the issue, according to Sarmento.France's fiscal pressureFrench government bond yields rose and the euro weakened on Monday as the unrest added to investor concerns over France's debt and budget."It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday."Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France. Fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said France faced a "very real risk" of a sovereign debt crisis."What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order; they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age... I mean, here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

schema.headline: What’s making Europe so angry? The frustration behind the protests

title: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet
description: watch nowAI is a transformational technology worth investing in — but investors must be selective when investing in data centers, according to the hea
body: watch nowAI is a transformational technology worth investing in — but investors must be selective when investing in data centers, according to the head of one of the world's biggest banks. Speaking to CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery called artificial intelligence "a major enabler to re-engineer and reimagine all our businesses, all our activities." "It's going to put a lot of power back in the hands of our colleagues because of the level of productivity it gives them, so it's going to be transformational, and we're certainly very much on a journey to adopt it," he said, adding that AI would help to "re-engineer the bank."But when it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, he advised discernment over an all-in approach."One has to be selective," Elhedery said. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."HSBC was ranked as the seventh-largest bank in the world and the biggest lender in Europe by S&P Global last year, with assets worth close to $3 trillion. The bank — headquartered in London — is both a financier and operator of data centers.In its 2025 annual report, HSBC said it intends to become "the leading bank for fast-growing transition ecosystems," noting that its customer base spans areas including data centers and the AI sector. Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing, and have seen a multibillion-dollar boom in recent years.Global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey, with Big Tech increasingly tapping private credit and taking on debt to fund the development of the facilities.But AI borrowing is becoming a source of tension in financial markets, as the cost of capital soars and corporations add to huge debt piles as they race to finance AI and the build-out of data centers. Speaking at LSEG and Eurasia Group's GZERO Summit in London earlier this month, Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic adviser of Allianz and former CEO of PIMCO, highlighted the competition for financing between governments and AI-related companies as a source of pressure in bond markets.  "Governments are borrowing what they're borrowing, plus they're refinancing debt at a higher level of rates," he said. "[And] you have hyperscalers who last year raised $200 billion in bond financing, and are probably going to raise a trillion in bond financing this year. They are yield insensitive. They are spread insensitive because they are betting on something that is truly transformational."Bond yields issued by various major economies have hit multi-decade highs in 2026, amid concerns around elevated government deficits and mounting debt levels alongside fears of sticky inflation and more hawkish central banks. JPMorgan Chase estimated earlier this year that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued by the end of the decade, as data center and other AI-adjacent companies splurge on building capacity.

schema.headline: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet

title: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom
description: watch nowSaudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and dro
body: watch nowSaudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks. The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement. The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured. Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser.CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh. This screen grab taken from CCTV footage played on a screen during a press conference by the Saudi-led coalition in Riyadh on October 15, 2026, and made available via AFPTV, shows what the coalition says was a Houthi attack on Abha International Airport on October 7, 2026. - | Afp | Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference  has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017. The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month. The Houthis claimed on Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport again; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces.The Saudi military destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson for the kingdom's armed forces said. Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom

title: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise
description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks during a midterm campaign rally at the LevelUp Training Complex on Oct. 15, 2026 in Monroe, Michigan.Pool | Getty
body: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks during a midterm campaign rally at the LevelUp Training Complex on Oct. 15, 2026 in Monroe, Michigan.Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesU.S. Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after President Donald Trump offered his backing for the leader's reelection bid next week.  "The president has the most effective endorsement in American or international political history," Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin's 2WAY Tonight published Monday. "I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on in the midterms," he said. Vance said he was not criticizing Netanyahu: "I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him," he said, adding that "I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Those remarks diverge from the approach by President Donald Trump, who gave the Israeli prime minister his backing in the election next week. Trump on Sunday praised Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, on Truth Social as "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran." In a social media post, Netanyahu thanked Trump for his "tremendous support and work together." Vance has weighed in on foreign politics before. He campaigned in Budapest in April to publicly endorse then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban's reelection bid. Orban was later voted out after 16 years in power. Last year in Munich for a security conference, Vance met Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party, which Elon Musk was also boosting at the time. The Israeli vote next week will be the first national election since Hamas attacked Israel in late 2023. The comments also come as U.S. public support for Israel, historically strong among both Republicans and Democrats, has fallen sharply. There has also been vigorous debate in America about the Netanyahu-led government's response to the Hamas attack.In June, Vance said that Israel has almost no friends left in the world and should think hard before turning on the one it has.

schema.headline: JD Vance refrains from endorsing Israeli leader Netanyahu as Trump offers praise

title: Data center stocks remain under pressure after Korea IPO plunges 30%
description: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesData center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a
body: Jonathan Raa | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesData center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave.Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity.The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities before some names clambered back into the green. CoreWeave shares are up 1.6% after dropping 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 1% while Iren was down about 4% in late morning trading.HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away."Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside.Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters. Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses.Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out.Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates.Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note.Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030."Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said.Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC."At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."

schema.headline: Data center stocks remain under pressure after Korea IPO plunges 30%

title: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
description: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person fami
body: Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.The agreement would cover a second 460-megawatt data center at the same West Virginia site as the first deal, the person said. The person asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the talks. The deal could be worth around $45 billion, the person said.CNBC reported the first deal in August.Bloomberg first reported that Anthropic and Nscale were in talks over a second deal. Anthropic declined to comment. Nscale has been approached for comment.AI infrastructure faces headwindsNvidia-backed Nscale is one of several companies that have emerged in recent years to develop the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence. The company builds or leases data centers and sells computing capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs.Rivals CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares drop 28% and 27%, respectively, in the past month, amid concerns over heavy borrowing.Nscale has faced its own challenges. On Sunday, U.K. newspaper The Telegraph reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid.An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site.""Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," the spokesperson added.The U.K.-based company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange in September.Anthropic's computing pushAnthropic said earlier this year that growing demand for its Claude AI models and products has caused "inevitable strain" on its infrastructure. Since then, it has announced a flurry of deals with infrastructure partners to try and increase its computing capacity, including major agreements with Advanced Micro Devices, Elon Musk's SpaceX, Google and  Broadcom.

schema.headline: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
